clue.text: Bowl of hot stuff with foul smell

parts.note: molten rock out of a volcano is about as hot as stuff gets
BO is body odour, two polite initials standing in for the smell

explanation.walkthrough: BO is the crossword's stock foul smell, and 'hot stuff' reads as innuendo until the volcano turns up. The bowl being defined is a church fitting, which is why the surface can ignore it.
explanation.definitionFit: A lavabo is the basin used for the ritual washing of hands at Mass, and by extension any washbasin.

clue.text: Underhand tactic, fudging flaw before time's up

indicators.note: To fudge something is to mess about with it until it is no longer straight, and letters treated that way will not stay as given.

parts.note: the four letters of FLAW, shuffled

indicators.note: One thing placed before another is written first, so this piece takes the top of a down entry.
The entry runs downwards, so a piece written 'up' is read from the bottom and arrives the other way round.

parts.note: an ERA is a stretch of time, climbing back up the column here

explanation.walkthrough: ERA is one of the crossword's workhorses for time, and it turns up climbing as often as the right way up. The word defined is a recent coinage: courts used the way weapons are.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawfare is attacking an enemy through lawsuits and legal process instead of weapons, so it wins by sly means rather than force.

clue.text: Early Porsche development: frontiers of UV waves on spyware

indicators.note: A frontier is where two territories meet, and these two words meet at the end of one and the start of the next.

parts.note: the letter standing at that word's border

indicators.note: In a down entry one thing sits on top of another, so this piece goes above — written first.

parts.note: the letter that word starts with, on the far side of the same border
a bug is the hidden microphone a spy plants

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface admits to being about letters — 'frontiers of UV waves' reads as physics. The car is the one Ferdinand Porsche drew up in the 1930s and the world bought by the million.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferdinand Porsche designed the original Volkswagen Beetle, nicknamed the Bug in America, decades before the sports cars carrying his name.

clue.text: Bane: where kidneys may be found?

parts.note: the same four letters in a different order — the clue prints the jumbled version and wants the tidy one

the same word a second time, for the other half: you need a word meaning 'mixed' that turns BEAN into 'Bane', and the answer supplies it — a salad is a mixture, so the answer is its own anagram indicator

explanation.walkthrough: The clue never says shuffle, because the answer says it: a salad is a mixture, so 'BEAN, mixed' is exactly the word the clue opens with. Setters call this reverse wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Kidney beans are the standard ingredient of such a dish, so the question mark asks you to read 'kidneys' as the pulse, not the organ.

clue.text: Outspoken choice to be in love with ring combatant

indicators.note: Something outspoken is said out loud, so it is the sound of the words that counts here and not their spelling.

parts.note: your pick is your choice, and the K vanishes once you write down only the sound
to adore is to be in love with, and the closing E is not sounded

explanation.walkthrough: Two ordinary English words said quickly run together into a Spanish one. 'Ring' is the trap — boxing first, bullfighting second — and only the answer settles which.
explanation.definitionFit: A picador is the horseman who lances the bull early in a bullfight, so the ring is the bullring and he does the fighting.

clue.text: Breathily said: 'Arsenic's taken and bootlegged'

indicators.note: What is taken is carried off, so the two letters named leave the longer word and do not come back.

parts.note: a consonant let out with a puff of breath is aspirated — the p at the start of 'pin'
As is the chemical symbol for arsenic, straight off the periodic table

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like reported speech. It is really one long word about pronunciation with a poison lifted out of the front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Bootlegged music is copied and sold without permission, which is what the word means in the trade in records, films and software.

clue.text: Stick ice cubes in prime minister's rear?

indicators.note: The rear of a thing is its back end, so only the closing stretch of the longer name is kept.

parts.note: Winston Churchill, Britain's wartime PM, whose name is long enough to carry a short word at its back

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark apologises for the liberty: no particular prime minister is named, so you try the famous ones until one of them ends in something meaning cool.
explanation.definitionFit: To chill a drink is to cool it, and dropping ice cubes into the glass is the quickest way of doing exactly that.

clue.text: Deadbeat, leaderless knight errant to pursue mobster? Duck!

indicators.note: A body with no leader has lost the one at its head, and a word's head is the letter at the front.
A knight errant wanders where he pleases, and letters that wander do not keep the order they came in.
To pursue is to come along behind, so this piece is written after the ones it chases.

parts.note: the head of a Mafia family is a don
a duck in cricket is a score of nought, written on the scoreboard as a zero
KNIGHT gives up its leading letter and the five that remain are jumbled

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket's duck for zero comes up constantly and is worth learning. The surface has a knight chasing a gangster, a picture from two different centuries that belongs to neither.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadbeat is an idler who never gets round to anything, and the answer is the older name for the same useless character.

clue.text: Withdraw from drunken trance

indicators.note: A drunk cannot walk in a straight line, and these letters will not keep to theirs either.

parts.note: six letters of fodder, exactly as the clue prints them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Withdraw from' reads as one phrase and wants to be the definition; only the first word is. The drink and the trance are scenery, and the letters were in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: To recant is to take back something you have publicly said or sworn, which is what withdrawing a statement or an accusation means.

clue.text: Probe small hovel?

parts.note: a pigsty, and by insult any filthy dwelling
-let is the ending that shrinks a thing: booklet, piglet, droplet

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the two halves say the same thing twice — a small sty — and the question mark admits it. The medical instrument has nothing to do with pigs.
explanation.definitionFit: A stylet is the fine wire or slender surgical probe a doctor runs down a needle or a catheter, so the two words name one instrument.

clue.text: Techie wordsmith holds advanced degree

indicators.note: What a thing holds is inside it, so the shorter piece is dropped into the middle of the longer one.

parts.note: Noah Webster wrote the American dictionary that still carries his name
MA is a Master of Arts, one step past a first degree

explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface belongs to a CV — techie, holds, advanced degree — and none of it is doing what it appears to. The lexicographer behind 'wordsmith' is the whole solve.
explanation.definitionFit: The person who builds and runs a website is a techie by trade, and the job title is the informal one the whole industry uses.

clue.text: Having special powers but uncrowned, like ancient Greeks

indicators.note: A crown sits on the head, so a word stripped of its crown gives up the letter at the front.

parts.note: bionic limbs give their owner powers no ordinary body has

explanation.walkthrough: Losing a crown sounds like abdication, which is why the word sits so comfortably next to the ancient world. It is only the first letter going.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionia was the Greek-settled coast of Asia Minor, and the adjective covers its people, their dialect and the order of column they built.

clue.text: Mr. Young's beef?

definitions.meaning: the guitarist in school uniform, Australian by upbringing and Scottish by name
the black cattle from the old Scottish county, and the steak they are raised for

explanation.walkthrough: The full stop after Mr marks the setter as American. Both halves are Scottish: a common first name that goes with the surname, and a breed named after the county.
explanation.definitionFit: Angus Young plays guitar in AC/DC, so a Mr Young may well be one; and Angus cattle are the breed prized for their steak.

clue.text: Language of sections of Rio eschewing contrived alliteration

indicators.note: A section is a part cut out of something, so it is the individual letters of the name that go, not the name as a block.
To eschew is to have nothing to do with something, so the fodder must manage without those letters.
Something contrived has been put together artificially, so what is left is arranged into an order it never had.

parts.note: twelve letters, and the raw material for everything that follows
R, I and O come out, each one taken from a different place in the twelve

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sections of Rio' reads as districts of a Brazilian city and 'contrived alliteration' as a complaint about the clue's own writing. Both are instructions, and the long word at the end is the material.
explanation.definitionFit: Late Latin is the written form used in the later Roman empire and the early church, a distinct stage of a tongue that lasted centuries.

clue.text: Renewal letter includes payment aid

indicators.note: What a thing includes is already inside it, so the letters are sitting in the clue in the order they are wanted.

parts.note: seven letters in a row, starting partway into the first word and stopping partway through the second

explanation.walkthrough: A renewal letter is such an ordinary piece of post that nothing about it asks to be read letter by letter, which is exactly the cover a hidden word wants.
explanation.definitionFit: The app that keeps your card details on a phone lets you pay by tapping it, which is help of a strictly financial kind.

clue.text: Defender in a game point

parts.note: the clue's own indefinite article, taken at face value
the four-letter game played on horseback, a crossword regular
the gist of an argument is its point

explanation.walkthrough: The modern sense of apology pulls the whole clue towards regret; the older sense, a reasoned defence of a position, is the one being defined. At four letters, try POLO for any game.
explanation.definitionFit: An apologist argues in defence of a cause or a doctrine, so the plain sense is meant and no saying sorry is involved.

clue.text: Remnants of reversal of Jewish ritual?

definitions.note: Debris is a mass noun taking a singular verb, but it names a scattered plurality, which is why a plural like 'remnants' defines it fairly.

parts.note: de- is the prefix that undoes a process: de-ice, de-frost, de-camp
a bris is the circumcision ceremony held on a boy's eighth day

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversal' looks like an instruction to turn letters round, and obeying it gets you nowhere. The word is being defined rather than obeyed: the setter wants the prefix meaning undo.
explanation.definitionFit: What is left lying about after something breaks up or is destroyed is exactly what the plural in the clue describes.

clue.text: Three vitamins removed from balanced diet, unwise fix-up

indicators.note: What is removed comes out and stays out, so those three letters are gone before anything else happens.
An unwise arrangement is a badly thought-out one — a loose way of saying the letters end up in no sensible order.

parts.note: twelve letters to start from, and the surface's picture of healthy eating
A, C and E are all vitamins, and all three come out

explanation.walkthrough: Take the vitamins out of a balanced diet and what is left spells, pleasingly, a bland one. Those nine letters then rearrange into the evening the definition describes.
explanation.definitionFit: In American usage a fix-up is an evening someone arranges between two people who have never met, which is the whole point of it.

clue.text: Blonde, blue-eyed detectives and Harry's pal lying about

indicators.note: Something left lying about has been dropped any old way up, so the assembled letters are read from the other end.

parts.note: the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the plain-clothes branch of a British police force
Ron Weasley, Harry Potter's best friend

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like Scandinavian television — blond detectives, something nasty in the snow — which is the genre the answer names. Harry Potter has given crosswords a reliable three-letter friend.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective covers Scandinavia and its people, and fair hair with pale eyes is the stereotype that travels with the word.

clue.text: Drug dealer shortened Eastern undergarment

indicators.note: A shortened word has had its end trimmed off, so the final letter never reaches the grid.

parts.note: a chemist in Britain is the pharmacist who dispenses drugs, docked of his last letter here
E is the compass abbreviation for eastern

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drug dealer' is a British chemist's shop rather than a street corner. It is the same joke every setter makes with the word, and worth expecting on sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemise is a loose slip worn next to the skin, so it goes under a dress rather than over it.

clue.text: Promiscuous sort of small bird?

parts.note: S is the clothing-label abbreviation for small
one that has wings, coined for the occasion — the question mark owns up to it

explanation.walkthrough: A winger is normally a footballer out on the flank. Here the word is taken back to its parts and handed to anything with wings, which is what the question mark apologises for.
explanation.definitionFit: A swinger is someone who swaps sexual partners freely, which is the loose living the surface is winking at.

clue.text: Obliterate vegetable

definitions.meaning: to flatten a thing out of existence, under a boot or a thumb
the gourd family, summer or winter, on every American table in autumn

explanation.walkthrough: Two words with nothing in common but their spelling, and the shortest clue in the puzzle. British solvers meet the vegetable sense less often than the drink of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is to crush something flat until nothing of it is left; the other is the American name for the marrow and pumpkin family.

clue.text: Moral of deviant: 'That's hilarious!'

indicators.note: A deviant has strayed from the straight path, and letters that stray end up in an order nobody intended.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder — the little 'of' is part of the material, not a joining word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' looks like joinery and is really part of the fodder, which is what makes the count come out. A clue about morals delivering internet slang is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The letters are texting shorthand for rolling on the floor laughing my ass off, typed in reply to something very funny indeed.

clue.text: PM expels head of monarchy, a rude sort

indicators.note: To expel is to throw out and refuse to have back, so the letter named is gone for good.

parts.note: Keir Starmer, the Labour leader who became British prime minister in 2024
the first letter of the word monarchy, its head

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a joke about a republican prime minister throwing out the crown. The mechanics are quieter: one name with a single letter lifted out of the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who gazes at strangers is being rude, and the noun for that person is formed the plain way, from the verb.

clue.text: Thick-headed Genevan philosopher's collection of bride's clothing

indicators.note: In the surface it is an insult; as an instruction it points at the head of the word 'thick', which is one letter.

parts.note: the letter standing at the head of THICK
Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712 and signed himself a citizen of it

explanation.walkthrough: Because Rousseau called himself a citizen of Geneva, the description is his own words. The insult at the front is aimed at nobody: it is there to hide a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A trousseau is the outfit of clothes and linen a woman assembles before her marriage, so the phrase names it precisely.

clue.text: Looms spinning at reduced speed

indicators.note: A spinning object shows a different face every moment, and letters treated so come to rest in a new order.

parts.note: five letters of fodder, and a weaving shed in the surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'Looms' wants to be a verb, something looming out of the fog. It is the weaver's machine, and it is the fodder: a plural noun doing an excellent impression of a threat.
explanation.definitionFit: The cutting-room shorthand for slow motion, the replay run at a fraction of the pace it was shot.

clue.text: Java, lacking kick, stood up to West

indicators.note: On an across entry the letters run westward when read the other way, from the right-hand end back to the left.

parts.note: to face someone down is to stand up to them

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is longer than it looks. 'Java' on its own would be coffee with all its caffeine present, so the comma and everything after it are doing necessary work.
explanation.definitionFit: Java is slang for coffee, and the version with its caffeine taken out is the one with no kick left in it.

clue.text: Around 5/9ths of what biorhythms are

indicators.note: Five ninths of a nine-letter word is its first five letters, counted from the front.

parts.note: body clocks run on a circadian rhythm, one turn of roughly a day

explanation.walkthrough: The fraction does arithmetic on a word the clue never prints: you have to supply the adjective for body clocks yourself, and only then start counting.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Latin for about, used before an uncertain date, and that is the sense of the English word here — approximately, not encircling.

clue.text: Beast with one horn that's deformed

indicators.note: Something deformed has been pushed out of its proper shape, and letters pushed about lose their proper order.

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
four letters of fodder, printed as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints the animal it defines, which is why the fodder is so hard to see. 'One' is the Roman numeral rather than a count of horns.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names any big wild animal, and this is one of them — the definition gives the class and the surface hints at the species.

clue.text: A migrant's developed popular app

indicators.note: To develop a site is to build something new on it, so nothing is left standing where it was.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, apostrophe and all

explanation.walkthrough: A migrant's story and a photo-sharing app have nothing to do with each other, which is the disguise. The count is exact, so the only work is spotting that 'developed' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The photo-sharing service has a couple of billion users, so calling it popular is understatement rather than opinion.

clue.text: Spa location uncovered in part of squalid digs

indicators.note: Take the cover off a word and the letter at the front comes away with it, leaving the rest exposed.
One piece goes inside the other rather than alongside it, which is what being in something means.

parts.note: an actor's part is a role
Bath, the Somerset city the Romans built their baths in, with its cover taken off

explanation.walkthrough: Two ordinary words are used in their less obvious senses at once: 'part' as a stage role, and 'Spa location' as an English city rather than a room in a hotel.
explanation.definitionFit: Digs is British for lodgings, and the answer is the standard insult for a filthy cramped place someone actually lives in.

clue.text: Faction of Minnesota legislature recalled dessert

indicators.note: A faction is one part of a larger body, so only a stretch of what follows is wanted.
To recall something is to call it back, and letters called back arrive in the opposite order.

parts.note: six letters in a row spanning the space between the two words, waiting to be read from the far end

explanation.walkthrough: State politics is a good place to hide an Italian pudding: nothing in a legislature asks to be read letter by letter, still less read from the wrong end.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian ice cream, churned slower and served warmer than the tub kind, and eaten at the end of a meal.
